articles.full_text:
AI News Tech Apple is racing to make Siri more agentic Future versions of Siri will be able to control third-party apps and perform more complex tasks.

Future versions of Siri will be able to control third-party apps and perform more complex tasks. by Terrence O'Brien Nov 8, 2026, 7:18 PM UTC Link Share Gift Photo: David Imel / The Verge Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor.

He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to accelerate the Siri roadmap and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI’s Dots or Meta’s Muse.

While Federighi has delivered a functional version of Siri AI on an incredibly short timeline, the company has no illusions that it’s keeping pace with its rivals.

Two significant improvements are expected to be made to Siri in the coming months.

One will give the assistant fine-grained control over Apple’s first-party apps, allowing it to do things like rotate and crop images in Photos and organize Safari tabs.

Those capabilities are expected to land with iOS 27.3.

The bigger change, integration with third-party apps, is likely to land later, in the Spring, according to Gurman.

That would let Siri place an order through Grubhub or book a dinner reservation through OpenTable, for example.

But that’s just the start.

Apple is expected to push Siri to become more agentic and enable features that will allow it to perform ongoing tasks, not just one-offs.

Gurman says: Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step.

Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.

articles.title: The great software IP writedown
articles.summary: Software's outsized margins were built on a scarcity of people who could build it. AI agents are removing that scarcity - so where does the value of software IP go?
articles.full_text:
Around a year ago I asked whether the cost of building software had just dropped 90% .

A lot has happened since then, and I've become more interested in the knock-on question: if building software is that much cheaper, what is the software itself actually worth?

Was software/SaaS a historic economic anomaly?

One thing that has become obvious to me researching this topic is that software is very much an outlier in terms of ability to extract outsized profit margins, and I think this fact underlines why the industry faces such existential challenges presently.

Typically in history you had three main ways of making "outsized" profits: Firstly, you had monopolistic behaviour, with Standard Oil being the textbook example.

While there are no doubt significant market competition concerns in software and SaaS, I would argue most software businesses, at least by number if not revenue, do not operate in a monopoly.

Secondly, you had network effects, restricting new market entrants.

Again, the tech giants clearly do have huge network effect benefits, but many smaller players do not, yet still make very healthy profit margins.

Newspapers (used to be) a good example of this, advertisers would want a readership base to advertise to, and if you were starting out from scratch with no readership base, you'd very much struggle to make the commercial model work without willingness to take heavy losses while you built up your readership.

Thirdly you had corruption or using violence to extract high profits out of your customers.

Protection money from the mafia is the obvious example historically (though still persists in some geographies).

Again, there is an argument that many software companies do achieve their market power via regulatory capture, especially in government contracting.

And many would argue regulatory capture is corruption with rounded corners.

But again, many software companies don't have a lobbying firm working for them, yet still do very well.

While you can argue that some of these factors are in play for certain tech companies, I struggle to see that the average small or mid-tier SaaS or software company takes advantage of this, yet posts usually extremely high gross (and often net) margins.

So why is this?

Intellectual scarcity I posit instead that these margins weren't driven by these mechanisms, but instead by simply not enough supply of people able to build software for the demand.

And while the number of people able to develop software has exploded over the past 20 or 30 years, the amount of software out there has equally exploded.

So in essence, market actors (whether that would be software engineers or companies) could derive a large amount of value for their work, because there is inherently a (fairly) small pool of people able to build said software.

You can see the issue though now AI agents can do a significant proportion of the engineering.

That scarcity is evaporating, which in this model therefore drives the value down sharply.

The market always beats margins out of you when there is a shift in supply.

Jevons paradox, though?

Of course, it's not quite as simple as AI agents can do coding, therefore the equilibrium between supply and demand changes.

Jevons paradox tells us that when something becomes cheaper and more efficient to use, we often end up using more of it, not less.

Jevons' original observation was that more efficient steam engines led to Britain burning more coal, not less.

So surely with a huge reduction in cost of bespoke software, we'll see far more demand.

This is true - we're seeing an absolute explosion in the amount of software being created.

But I'd argue this software is intrinsically different to what made SaaS (especially) so valuable.

The rough idea with SaaS was that you spent some money on development, and then could sell the same software to thousands or millions of customers.

Your marginal cost of a new customer was close to zero, at least in terms of software costs.

But with the Jevons paradox-induced software we have now, it is incredibly bespoke for the most part.

Why use a generic CRM when you could build (or purchase) one designed for your exact domain?

I think this dynamic explains the real issue here.

Yes , there will be software products in the future.

But I suspect these software products will be for the most part far smaller in addressable market size.

Baumol's cost disease Of course, an argument could be that future software companies operate hundreds or thousands of distinct products, across a whole bunch of markets.

There is no doubt with agents this could be from a technology point of view at least more possible than before.

But I think the flaw with this strategy is Baumol's cost disease .

When productivity shoots up in one part of the economy, the parts that can't speed up end up getting relatively more expensive.

The classic example is a string quartet, which needs the same four musicians and the same amount of time as it did in 1800.

Apply that to a software business and the bottleneck moves very quickly from building the product to selling it.

Already I'm seeing that while building software has got 10x quicker, sales and marketing is as slow as it always was, at least for most B2B deals.

So I think this explains the flaw with the "software factory" concept that many have been pushing.

Yes, you can build hundreds of line-of-business applications in a fraction of the time, if you really want to.

But selling these to actual humans is just as hard in my opinion, despite the claims of many that they've managed to automate go to market - any (questionable) efficiencies of these approaches are outweighed by the fact that each buyer has far more marketing directed at them.

I therefore think that there is certainly going to be a market for SaaS in the future - not everyone is going to vibe code their own apps, though some will.

But my gut tells me that these are going to be far smaller in scale - and therefore the underlying VC model of throw loads of cash at a SaaS business to scale as fast as possible is even more broken than it was before.

Reproduction The final thing that is really nagging at me is just how easy it is to copy software now.

You can take any agent, give it some screenshots (or if you are even more lazy, a browser tab for it to control) and tell it to clone software you think you like.

We've already seen this on an industrial scale with the ArtCraft suite of clones of everything from Excel to Photoshop.

While I'm sure they are not quite as good or stable as the "genuine" product, this has been the biggest shock to me.

Arguably already their Photoshop clone has more features than the unfortunately named GIMP open source clone of Photoshop, which has had 30 years of human effort aimed at it.

So this again makes me wonder where the value in software IP lives.

Certainly agents aren't (yet) capable of coming up with good software products to build a business around, so there is definitely value in product taste and choosing the right product to build.

But if you do find a successful niche for your product, it is now trivial for anyone to copy that.

So this makes me question exactly where the value is going to lie in future.

One other thing I've noticed is that it's much easier to move between software providers now.

Agents can export your data, transform it and import it into a new tool very easily.

Even if the provider doesn't offer a nice export, agents are very capable of reverse engineering the web app and doing the export for you anyway.

Switching costs have always been one of the quieter moats in SaaS, and that moat is draining too.

The writedown This is where I think it gets uncomfortable for the finance side.

For the past decade or so, the standard defence of loss-making software companies has been that R&D isn't really an expense.

It's an investment.

You spend heavily on engineering today, and you get a long-lived asset - the product - that keeps paying out for years.

That logic only holds if the R&D actually builds something durable.

If a competitor - or your own customer - can rebuild what you spent five years on in a few weeks with agents, then that spend isn't building an asset at all.

It's much closer to a running cost you have to keep paying just to stand still.

Which means the underlying economics of a lot of software companies are quite a bit worse than the adjusted numbers suggest.

You can see the same thing from the M&A side.

A lot of tech acquisitions were really build-vs-buy decisions.

Paying 10x revenue for a startup made sense when building the equivalent in-house would take two years and 30 engineers.

But if your own team, with agents, can build it in a matter of weeks, the premium for the technology itself drops to close to zero.

You're only paying for the customers and the distribution - and if the product has no real traction, the IP on its own is worth roughly what it would cost to rebuild.

Which is not very much anymore.

A year ago I was asking whether the cost of building software had dropped 90%.

I think the more uncomfortable question now is whether the value of what's already been built has dropped by a similar amount.

articles.title: Meta says US users can now video chat with their Muse AI avatar
articles.summary: Meta's AI agent can now take calls as a customizable animated avatar, ahead of the launch of a Tamagotchi-like wearable designed to bring Muse to life.
articles.full_text:
Muse Voice, a feature that lets users call and video chat with Meta’s consumer AI agent, Muse, is now available to everyone in the U.S., the company announced on Thursday.

First introduced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September, the video-chatting feature involves new AI models, Muse Realtime Avatar and Muse Realtime Voice technology, which help power the digital avatar that chats with the user.

While other AI competitors offer voice chat features, Meta’s Muse offers a cute, animated avatar (nicknamed Jolly), which users interact with as they ask questions or request tasks to be handled on their behalf.

Users can also customize the avatar as they choose, changing it to something that looks more like a person, animal, or some other character.

The company believes that anthropomorphizing Muse in this way could make consumers feel more connected to their AI agent — a connection that could grow even stronger as they begin to engage in live conversations with it.

As the Muse avatar speaks, Meta says it will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that match the tone of the conversation. (Muse doesn’t actually “see” the user, but it hears them and reacts based on their conversations.) The news of the rollout was announced via blog post and on X by Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, who shared a demo of his Muse in action.

The video saw Wang joking around, referencing his love of posting memes on X, which he told his Muse may have gotten him in trouble with his boss.

His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!) The added support for video chats and calls comes just before Meta’s plan to launch a Tamagotchi-like wearable device for its Muse AI agent before year-end.

When the device arrives, the digital avatar will appear on its small screen, letting users talk to the agent, which can then reply or carry out tasks for them.

Meta says the real-time conversations are supported on mobile, web, and Mac and will later come to its AI Glasses and the upcoming “Muse Charm” hardware device.
